sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Raijin** ​(*raijin*) — ‌Thunder, Lightning ‌· Drum-riding ​lord ​of storms ​— belongs ​to the ​Japanese ‌tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Thunder, ‌Lightning". The ​name means ‌"Thunder god"[^1].

​**Raijin** ​is the ​thunder god ​of Japan, ​a ‌fierce, demon-like ​kami who ‌beats drums ​to ‌create thunder ​and hurls ‌lightning bolts. ​He ‌is the ​counterpart of ​Fūjin, the ‌wind god, ‌and ‌the two ​are often ​depicted together ‌at ​the gates ​of Buddhist ‌temples, where ​their ​terrifying forms ‌ward off ​evil. Beneath ‌the ​demon mask ​lives one ​of Japan's ​oldest ‌powers: thunder, ‌the voice ​of the ‌dead ​world breaking ​into ours.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as ‌**Raijin** and ​serves its ‌temple at ​[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/raijin/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form — ​a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*raijin* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Japanese ​characters ​as ​**雷神**. ​Etymologically ‌it means ​"Thunder ​god"[^1].

‌The ​ASCII ‌form ​*raijin* survives ‌only ​because ​the ​early ​domain-name ​system could ‌not ​carry ‌diacritics; ​it ‌is a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not ‌an ​ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ‌restoration ‌**Raijin** ​recovers ​the ‌full diacritic ​detail ​of ‌the ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly in ​the ‌address ​bar. ​The ​restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ‌— ‌a ​description ‌computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- **r** ​→ ​**R** ​— ‌Same, ​capitalized
- **a** ​→ ​**a** ‌— ​Same
- ​**i** ​→ **i** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**j** ​→ ‌**j** ​— Same
- ‌**i** ‌→ ​**i** ​— ​Same
- ​**n** → ‌**n** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is ​**/ɾa.i.dʑiɴ/** — ​Modern ​Standard Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

Phoneme ‌by ​phoneme:

- **Rai-** ​— ‌Alveolar tap ​[ɾ], ‌open central ​[a], ‌close front ​[i]; ​from 雷 ​'thunder'
- ​**-jin** — ​Voiced ‌alveolo-palatal affricate ​[dʑ], close ‌front ​[i], moraic ‌nasal ​[ɴ]; from ‌神 ​'god/spirit'

For ‌the ​modern speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ‌is: ‌'RAH-ee-jeen' — ​the ​'r' is ‌a light ​tap, ​and the ‌final ​'n' is ​a ‌soft nasal.

​Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ​of the ​name:

- ​**Japanese** — ‌雷神 (Raijin), ‌'Thunder ​God'
- **Pairing** ‌— ​Fūjin, the ​wind ‌god — ‌born, ‌like Raijin, ‌from ​Izanagi's purification ‌breath ​(Kojiki)
- **Indian ​counterpart** ​— Indra, ‌the Vedic ​thunderer, ​mediated through ​Buddhist ‌Taishakuten

Raijin ​keeps ​its restoration ​plain: ‌plain Hepburn. ​He ‌is the ​thunder ‌god, often ​paired ‌with Fūjin ‌at temple ​gates; ​the script ​has ​no diacritic ‌the ‌ASCII form ​loses.

sections.body:
**Raijin** ​is the ‌thunder god ‌of ​Japan, a ​fierce, demon-like ​kami ​who beats ​drums to ‌create ​thunder and ​hurls lightning ‌bolts. He ​is ‌the counterpart ​of Fūjin, ‌the ​wind god, ​and the ​two ​are often ​depicted together ‌at ​the gates ‌of Buddhist ​temples, ‌where their ​terrifying forms ‌ward ​off evil. ‌Beneath the ​demon ​mask lives ‌one of ‌Japan's oldest ‌powers: ​thunder, the ​voice of ‌the ​dead world ​breaking into ‌ours.[^1]

### ​Thunder Drummer

​He beats ‌drums ​set around ‌his body ​to ​produce thunder; ​the number ​of ‌rings on ‌the drums ​counts ‌the storm's ​strength.

### Lightning ​Hurling

He ‌casts ‌lightning in ‌the shape ‌of ​arrows or ‌writhing thunder-snakes ​from ​the storm ​clouds.

### Fūjin's ‌Companion

​Paired with ​the wind ​god ‌in temple ​art and ​architecture ​for more ‌than a ​thousand ‌years.

### Demon ​Guardian

His ‌fierce form ​protects ‌temples from ‌harmful influences; ​as ​one of ​the Twelve ​Devas ‌he guards ‌the Dharma ​itself.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Raijin ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**Thunder drums** ​— ​The ‌ring ​of ‌drums ​around ‌his ​body; ‌each ​beat ‌of ​thunder is ​a ‌drumstroke, ‌and ‌the ​rings ​on ‌the ​drumheads ​count ‌them
- ​**Lightning ​bolts** ‌— The ​arrows ‌or ​thunder-snakes ​(raiki) ​he ​casts ‌from ‌the ​clouds
- ‌**Demon ​face** ​— ‌His fierce ‌oni ‌expression ‌— ​the ‌standard ​visual ​grammar ​of ‌Japanese ​protective ​deities, ​whose ugliness ‌is ​a ​shield
- ​**Storm ‌clouds** ​— ‌The ​dark ‌clouds ​from ‌which ‌he ​emerges, drawn ​as ​a ​floating ‌island ‌of ​thunder

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Raijin's mythology is a palimpsest: ​the thunder kami of the *Kojiki*, the Buddhist ‌guardian of esoteric temple art, the storm god ‌of the Mongol-invasion legend, and the bogey of ​nursery warnings — four layers of one drumbeat. ​The sources are layered and partly at odds, and ​each layer tells us what thunder meant to ​a different Japan.[^1]

### Thunder Born of the Dead ​Goddess (Kojiki)

In the *Kojiki*, Izanami dies from ‌the burns of the fire god Kagutsuchi, and ​her grieving husband Izanagi pursues her into Yomi, the ​land of the dead. When he breaks his ‌promise not to look, he sees her body ​corrupted; in her fury Izanami sends the **yakusa ‌no ikazuchi** — the eight thunder spirits — ​in pursuit, together with the hags of Yomi. ‌The text explains that these thunderers were born from ​the filth of Izanami's dying body. Izanagi escapes ​at the Even Pass of Yomotsu Hirasaka and ​seals the way with a boulder. Thunder, then, ​is older than the cleanly born gods: it ​issues from death itself, from the corruption of the ‌beloved. Fūjin, by contrast, is born later, from ​Izanagi's breath during his river purification — wind ‌as the breath of the purified, thunder as ​the voice of the dead. The later Buddhist ‌painters gave this archaic terror his demon drums and ​his cloud-island, but the *Kojiki* keeps the older ‌truth: **the storm speaks with the voice of ​the world we have lost.**[^2]

### Guardian of the ‌Dharma (Buddhist adoption)

With the arrival of esoteric ​Buddhism, the thunder power was enrolled in the defenses ​of the Dharma. From the Heian period, Raijin ‌appears among the **Jūni-ten**, the Twelve Devas who ‌guard the four directions and the zenith and ‌nadir of the mandala, and with Fūjin he ​comes to stand at temple gatehouses — the pair ​most famously at the great Nioh-mon gates of ‌Zen temples, where their sculpted forms confront visitors ​with the storm itself. His drumbeats scatter demons; ​his lightning burns away obstacles; his ugliness is ‌itself a weapon, since in Buddhist iconography the fierce ​faces (the same grammar as the Nioh guardians) ​are shields that frighten evil before it can ‌enter. Native kami and Buddhist guardian are not ​rivals here but one figure read twice: the ‌*Kojiki*'s thunderer and the mandala's defender are the ​same sound heard through two theologies. **Japan's thunder god ​guards the gate because thunder has always guarded ​the boundary between worlds.**

### Raijin and the Mongol ​Storms (The Divine Wind)

In 1274 and again ‌in 1281, typhoons destroyed the invasion fleets Kublai ‌Khan sent against Japan. The warrior Takezaki Suenaga, who ​fought in both campaigns, commissioned the picture-scroll *Mōko ‌Shūrai Ekotoba* (c. 1293), whose final scenes show ​the fleet shattered and drowning in the tempest. ​Medieval chronicles credited the court's prayers to Hachiman ‌and Amaterasu, but in the popular imagination the storms ‌were the direct work of the storm gods ‌— Raijin drumming the clouds open above the ‌strait while Fūjin filled them with wind. Later ​tradition named the typhoons **kamikaze**, the 'divine wind'. ‌The legend grew into one of Japan's foundational stories ​of being saved by the gods, invoked again ​in the twentieth century — for catastrophic ends ​— as proof that the islands enjoyed supernatural ‌protection. Whatever the theology, the myth records a ​real memory: **that the sea between Japan and the ​continent belongs to the storm gods**, and that ​they have defended it before.

### Thunder and the ‌Navel (Folk belief)

Japanese folk belief holds that ​Raijin eats the navels of children. During thunderstorms, ​parents ordered children to cover their bellies — *heso ​o kakusu* — and the custom persists idiomatically ‌today, where covering the navel is also said ​to prevent catching cold. Behind the bogey lies ‌an older logic: the navel is the body's ​center and its first scar, the mark of ‌the cut that began independent life, and in folk ​anatomy it is the belly that illness and ‌hunger strike first. Lightning, the sky's predator, seeks ‌the exposed center of life just as thunder ​frightens the body's center of courage. The belief ​turns Raijin into the most domestic of terrors — ​not a god of cosmic battles but the ​reason a child clutches a blanket in a ‌storm. **The thunder god lives in the nursery ‌because that is where fear is taught, and ​where protection is first learned.**

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Raijin ​descends from ‌Indian ‌Indra through ​the ​Buddhist Taishakuten, ​but ​he is ​no ‌simple borrowing: ​the ​*Kojiki*'s thunder ‌spirits ​born of ‌Izanami's ​body are ‌native ​and older, ​and ​the mature ​Raijin ​is the ‌fusion ​of both ‌lines. ​In esoteric ‌Buddhism ​he serves ‌among ​the Twelve ‌Devas, ​and his ​permanent ‌pairing with ‌Fūjin ‌expresses the ​Japanese ​reading of ‌storms ​as coupled ​powers ‌— wind ​and ​thunder — ‌rather ​than as ‌one ​god's attribute. ​The ​medieval kamikaze ​legend ‌added a ‌third ​layer, national ‌salvation; ​the nursery ​warning ‌a fourth, ‌domestic ‌discipline. Each ‌tradition ​kept the ‌same ​figure because ​each ​needed the ‌same ​thing: a ​way ​to say ‌that ​the storm ​is ​not random.[^1]

‌Kindred ​figures in ‌the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index ​include [[adad|Adad]], ‌[[baal|Baꜥal]], ‌[[enlil|Enlīl]], [[illapa|Illapa]], ​[[keraunos|Keraunós]], ​and [[marduk|Marduk]], ​each ​linked through ‌thunder ‌/ storm ​sovereignty.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Raijin ​remains ‌one of ‌Japan's ​most ​visually ​striking deities. ​His ​most ‌famous ​portrait, Tawaraya ​Sōtatsu's ‌*Fūjin-Raijin-zu* ​screens ‌(early seventeenth ​century, ‌now ​a ​National Treasure ​at ​Kennin-ji ​in ‌Kyoto), is ​a ‌canonical ​image ‌of Japanese ​art, ‌endlessly ​reproduced. ‌The Kaminarimon ​— ​'Thunder ‌Gate' ‌— of ‌Sensō-ji ​in ​Asakusa ‌has guarded ​the ​temple ‌approach ​since 942, ​its ‌great ​red ‌lantern one ​of ​Tokyo's ​landmarks. ​He drums ‌his ‌way ​through ‌ukiyo-e, manga, ​anime, ​and ‌video ‌games as ‌the ‌archetype ​of ‌overwhelming natural ​power, ​and ​the ‌old folk ​instruction ​to ​cover ‌one's navel ​in ​a ​storm ‌is still ​spoken ‌to ​Japanese ‌children. Few ​gods ‌so ‌terrifying ​in appearance ​live ​so ​comfortably ‌in a ‌modern ​city.[^1]

sections.body: Raijin's ​material ‌record ‌is ​pictorial and ​architectural ​rather ​than ​inscriptional. ‌The ​supreme ​witness ‌is Tawaraya ​Sōtatsu's ‌*Fūjin-Raijin-zu* ​(early ‌seventeenth ​century, ​ink ​and ​color on ​paper, ‌National ​Treasure, ‌Kennin-ji, ​Kyoto), ‌which ​fixed ‌the modern ​image ‌of ​the ​drum-ringed ‌thunderer. ‌The ‌Kaminarimon ​('Thunder Gate') ​of ‌Sensō-ji, ​Asakusa, ​first ‌built ​in ​942 ‌and rebuilt ​in ‌1960 ​after ​the ​1865 ​fire, ‌enshrines ‌Fūjin and ​Raijin ‌statues ​above ​its ‌famous ‌lantern. ‌Sets ‌of the ​Twelve ‌Devas ​(Jūni-ten) ​at ​esoteric ‌temples ​such ​as Tō-ji ​in ‌Kyoto ​preserve ​Heian-period ​sculptural ‌lineages ​of ‌the thunder ​guardian, ‌and ​Hokusai's ‌manga ‌sketches ​spread ​his ​likeness to ​every ‌corner ‌of ​Japan.[^1]

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Raijin ​is the ‌sound of ‌the ​sky's anger ​and ​the light ​that splits ​the ‌darkness. He ​reminds ​us that ‌nature is ​not ‌merely beautiful; ​it ‌is also ​loud, dangerous, ​and ​alive. To ​stand ​before Raijin ‌is to ​feel ‌small before ​the ‌storm — ​and Japan, ‌sitting ​in the ‌typhoon ​belt on ​the Pacific ‌Ring ‌of Fire, ‌has ​more reason ​than most ‌civilizations ​to keep ​that ‌feeling close.

​Yet the ​same ‌tradition that ​made ‌him a ​demon made ​him ​a guardian. ​The ‌drum that ‌terrifies the ​child ‌also warns ​the ​temple; the ‌lightning that ‌burns ‌the tree ‌also ​marks the ‌god who ​protects ​the gate. ​Raijin ‌holds both ​truths without ​embarrassment. ​In an ‌age ​that likes ​to separate ​danger ‌from safety, ​he ‌is the ​older, wiser ‌figure: ​the same ‌sky ‌does both, ​and the ​wise ​household covers ​its ‌navel and ‌keeps its ​gate.[^1]
